title: Verifiable Sampling for Delegated Generative Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Matteo Inajetovic, Anna Pappa, Petros Wallden
abstract: Generative machine learning has shown remarkable results across a wide range of interdisciplinary tasks, motivating significant efforts toward Quantum Generative Models as a path to beyond-classical performance, given their capability of generating classically intractable distributions. However, comparatively little attention has been paid to securely delegating such computations to a powerful remote quantum server. In this work, we propose a blind and verifiable protocol for sampling that can be used for the inference phase of such quantum models. Such a protocol inherits blindness from Universal Blind Quantum Computing and achieves verifiability by exploiting known approaches based on trapification schemes. Alongside, to delegate the training phase, we discuss an extension of the previously proposed verifiable end-to-end Delegated Variational Quantum Algorithms (Inajetovic et al., Phys. Rev. Research, 2026).   Beyond the usual Accept/Abort outcome characterizing verification protocols, the sampling protocol for inference also provides, even against a malicious server, an estimation of the amount of corrupted generated samples, i.e., a fine-grained feature describing the quality of the outcome connecting verification protocols and application-level benchmarking.
summary: This paper presents a novel, blind, and verifiable protocol for sampling from Quantum Generative Models when the computation is outsourced to a remote quantum server. It achieves security by combining techniques from blind quantum computing with trapification to detect malicious corruption. Crucially, the protocol moves beyond a simple pass/fail check by estimating the precise fraction of corrupted samples, offering a quantitative quality assessment for delegated quantum tasks.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of securely delegating the sampling phase of Quantum Generative Models (QGMs) to a remote quantum server while ensuring verifiability against malicious behavior.
main_result: They propose a blind and verifiable sampling protocol that not only detects malicious corruption but also provides a fine-grained estimation of the exact amount of corrupted samples, $\gamma$.
method: The protocol combines principles from Universal Blind Quantum Computing and utilizes trapification schemes to achieve verifiability, allowing for error bounding based on distance metrics like MMD, TVD, and DKL.
model_or_system: The work focuses on Quantum Generative Models (QGMs) used for generating complex distributions, building upon concepts from Quantum Circuit Born Machines (QCBMs) and general quantum computation graphs.
key_observables: The key observables include the estimated corrupted sample ratio ($\gamma$), trap detections (TD), and the resulting confidence interval $[\gamma_l, \gamma_u]$ for the true corruption rate.
important_parameters: Key parameters include the number of computation rounds ($d$), test rounds ($t$), and the maximum tolerable corruption ratio ($\gamma_{\max}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the existence of a suitable distance function $L$ allowing for linear factorization in $\gamma$, and for verifiable optimization, it assumes all gradient evaluations share the same MBQC graph.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the correlation between trap detections and wrong samples, while Table I presents numerical results for delegated inference under a Malicious Noise Model Attack.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the need for secure delegation for QGMs, then details the Verifiable Sampling Protocol (Protocol 2) for inference, and finally extends this framework to provide verifiable end-to-end training for QGMs.
why_interesting: While focused on quantum computation security, the rigorous error bounding techniques and the development of quantifiable quality metrics ($\gamma$ estimation) are highly relevant for any quantum algorithm implementation where noise or adversarial attacks are a concern.
